China raised concerns of judicial overreach after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying on Friday “such practices are not conducive” to a resolution. Beijing’s statement comes after the top UN court determined Myanmar’s deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority amounted to genocide. China is a rare enduring partner for Myanmar after Min Aung Hlaing’s 2021 coup, which prompted Western nations to cut ties with the Southeast Asian nation. “China is concerned about issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation, and believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue,” he added. Xue “expressed views based on international law and the facts of the case while drawing on professional experience… which also demonstrates a commitment to fulfilling duties”, he said. The ruling was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ determined a state had committed genocide. More than a million Rohingya live in Bangladesh, most having fled the brutal 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar. The ICJ also ordered refugees be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urging Myanmar to allow those exiled to return home.
